title: Trust a model change you didn't write
summary: A teammate's agent retrains a model and claims a big gain. A reviewer who never reads the training code checks the claim with run records, a join on customer ids, a clean holdout and a guarded write.
source: A recorded run of the real tools, replayed, on synthetic data (examples/model-review/make_data.py): nothing here measures a real service.

steps.note: Reviewer: before judging a model, is the frozen holdout like the data it will be judged against? Compare the churn rate and tenure.
steps.cmd: for f in train holdout; do stats describe $f.csv --cols tenure_months,churned > $f.json; echo "$f: churn rate $(jsonq -p /data/columns/1/mean --format text $f.json), mean tenure $(jsonq -p /data/columns/0/mean --format text $f.json)"; done
steps.out:
train: churn rate 0.59, mean tenure 30.5
holdout: churn rate 0.53, mean tenure 30.5

steps.note: Teammate's agent: the model in production uses tenure only. I trained a forest on every feature, and tracked both runs. (The PR's claim: accuracy 0.977 against 0.758.)
steps.cmd: ml fit --model logistic --target churned --drop id,monthly_spend,tickets_90d --track runs --output prod/model.ml train.csv > /dev/null; ml fit --model forest --task classification --target churned --drop id --track runs --output cand.ml candidate_train.csv > /dev/null; ml runs list runs > runs.json; echo "$(ls runs | wc -l) run records"

steps.note: Reviewer: what do the run records say about each run?
steps.cmd: for i in 0 1; do echo "$(jsonq -p /data/runs/$i/model --format text runs.json) trained on $(jsonq -p /data/runs/$i/train_rows --format text runs.json) rows, scored on $(jsonq -p /data/runs/$i/metrics_on --format text runs.json)"; done
steps.out:
"logistic" trained on 400 rows, scored on "train"
"forest" trained on 480 rows, scored on "train"

steps.note: Compare them: the inputs that differ, and the headline numbers. The new model had 80 more training rows, and the 0.977 is a score on training data.
steps.cmd: A=$(jsonq -p /data/runs/0/id --format text runs.json | tr -d '"'); B=$(jsonq -p /data/runs/1/id --format text runs.json | tr -d '"'); ml runs compare runs $A $B > cmp.json; echo "training rows $(jsonq -p /data/inputs/3/a --format text cmp.json) -> $(jsonq -p /data/inputs/3/b --format text cmp.json)"; echo "accuracy $(jsonq -p /data/metrics/0/a --format text cmp.json) -> $(jsonq -p /data/metrics/0/b --format text cmp.json)"

steps.note: Where did the 80 extra rows come from? A join on customer id: how many of the candidate's training customers are in the frozen holdout?
steps.cmd: table --query "select count(*) as overlap from 'candidate_train.csv' as a inner join 'holdout.csv' as b on a.id = b.id" | jsonq -p /data/rows/0/0 --format text -

steps.note: So 80 of the 200 holdout customers were trained on. An anti join leaves the customers neither model has seen.
steps.cmd: table --query "select b.id, b.tenure_months, b.monthly_spend, b.tickets_90d, b.churned from 'holdout.csv' as b anti join 'candidate_train.csv' as a on b.id = a.id" --format csv > clean_holdout.csv; peek --count-lines --lines 1:1 clean_holdout.csv | jsonq -p /data/total_lines --format text -

steps.note: Score on customers it never saw. The honest gain is smaller than the claim, but it is real.
steps.cmd: echo "production, clean holdout            $(ml eval --model-file prod/model.ml clean_holdout.csv --drop id,monthly_spend,tickets_90d | jsonq -p /data/metrics/accuracy --format text -)"; echo "candidate, full holdout (leaked)     $(ml eval --model-file cand.ml holdout.csv --drop id | jsonq -p /data/metrics/accuracy --format text -)"; echo "candidate, clean holdout             $(ml eval --model-file cand.ml clean_holdout.csv --drop id | jsonq -p /data/metrics/accuracy --format text -)"
steps.out:
production, clean holdout            "0.725"
candidate, full holdout (leaked)     "0.895"
candidate, clean holdout             "0.85"

chart.title: Accuracy: the claim against what the review found

steps.note: Teammate's agent: retrained on the training file only, tracked. Reviewer: the run record can be replayed, and the clean holdout is the test.
steps.cmd: ml fit --model forest --task classification --target churned --drop id --track runs --output cand2.ml train.csv > fit3.json; R=$(jsonq -p /data/run/id --format text fit3.json | tr -d '"'); echo "replay verifies: $(ml runs verify runs $R | jsonq -p /data/verified --format text -)"; echo "clean holdout accuracy $(ml eval --model-file cand2.ml clean_holdout.csv --drop id | jsonq -p /data/metrics/accuracy --format text -)"
steps.out:
replay verifies: true
clean holdout accuracy "0.8666666666666667"

steps.note: Promote it, guarded: the write only happens if production still holds the file the reviewer looked at.
steps.cmd: H=$(env hash --root prod model.ml --format text | cut -d' ' -f1); write --root prod --if-sha256 $H --stdin model.ml < cand2.ml > promote.json; echo "promoted: $(jsonq -p /data/changed --format text promote.json), now $(jsonq -p /data/after_sha256 --format text promote.json)"; echo $H > old_hash.txt

steps.note: Another agent, which read production before this promotion, tries to promote the original, leaked candidate. The write is refused, and says what the file holds now.
steps.cmd: write --root prod --if-sha256 $(cat old_hash.txt) --stdin model.ml < cand.ml > stale.json; jsonq -p /error/rule --format text stale.json; jsonq -p /error/detail/actual_sha256 --format text stale.json

steps.note: Reviewer: what may each tool do? The compilers proved it, and none of them reaches the network.
steps.cmd: for t in ml table stats write hash; do echo "$t $(env $t introspect | jsonq -p /authority/effects --format text -)"; done
